# Project Management {#sec-git}

Git records the history of a project so that an analyst can work reproducibly,
recover from mistakes, and collaborate without exchanging unnamed copies of
files. GitHub and similar services host Git repositories online; they add
backup, discussion, and review around Git's local history. This chapter
introduces the ideas and commands needed for the projects in this book. The
free *Pro Git* book provides a fuller reference [@chacon2014progit].

Several hands-on resources complement this chapter. The [Git and GitHub for
Beginners crash course](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RGOj5yH7evk) provides a
visual overview, [Git Exercises](https://gitexercises.fracz.com/) offers
short command-line practice, and [Oh My Git!](https://ohmygit.org/) teaches
Git through an open-source game. Version control is useful beyond Git because
it preserves history, supports recovery, and coordinates work across
collaborators. Hofert's beginner-friendly tutorial compares the fundamentals
of Git and Subversion and is a useful additional reading
[@hofert2025version]. Use all of these resources for practice, but check each
command against `git status` and the repository's documentation.

GitHub is one hosting service for Git repositories; [Bitbucket](https://bitbucket.org/)
and [GitLab](https://gitlab.com/) offer similar services. Hosting a repository
online provides a backup of committed work and makes collaboration with
classmates and coworkers easier.

## The Git Model

A Git repository is a project directory together with a database of its
history. The **working tree** contains files being edited, the **staging area**
records changes intended for the next snapshot, and a **commit** stores that
snapshot with an author, time, and message. Thinking in these three states
prevents the common mistake of treating `git add` as a backup or `git commit`
as an upload.

The staging area makes a commit a deliberate unit of work. You can inspect a
change, stage only the part that belongs together, and then commit a coherent
snapshot. A good commit should explain one change in the imperative mood, such
as `content: clarify relative paths`; generated files, credentials, and large
local data should not be committed.

## Installing and Configuring Git

Install Git before creating a repository. Use [Git for
Windows](https://gitforwindows.org/) on Windows, and use the package manager or
installer appropriate for macOS or Linux; the official [Git downloads
page](https://git-scm.com/downloads) lists current options
[@git-scm2025downloads]. On Windows, open **Git Bash** for the Unix-style
commands used in this book.

Git needs an identity so that each commit records who made it, and a remote
account provides a place to share those commits. Set your local name and email
once on a computer, then verify the values:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --list --show-origin
```

An account on GitHub is separate from a local Git installation. Set up GitHub
by creating an account, generating an SSH key if you do not already have one,
and adding the key's public half to your GitHub account; HTTPS authentication
is an alternative. GitHub's onboarding guide explains account setup and
authentication [@github2025gettingstarted].

## A First Local Workflow

The safest beginner workflow is to inspect, stage, inspect again, and then
commit. Start by cloning an existing repository or initializing a new one:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/OWNER/REPOSITORY.git
cd REPOSITORY

# For a new local project instead:
git init
```

`git status` is the most useful diagnostic command. It reports the current
branch, changed files, staged files, and files Git is ignoring. Run it before
and after each logical operation rather than guessing what Git will do. The
following sequence records a small change:

```bash
git status
git diff                 # changes not yet staged
git add path/to/file.qmd
git diff --staged        # changes that will enter the commit
git commit -m "content: explain the Git workflow"
git status
```

`git add` copies the selected version into the staging area; it does not send
anything to GitHub. `git commit` saves the staged snapshot locally; it does not
publish it. `git push` is the operation that sends local commits to a remote.
This distinction is the foundation of a reliable backup and collaboration
workflow.

Beginners should avoid `git add .` because it stages every unignored change
below the current directory, including files they may not have inspected or
intended to commit. Stage named files, such as `git add 02-git.qmd`, and review
`git diff --staged` before committing. Use `git add .` only when you have
deliberately checked every change in the directory.

The seven commands used most often in this book are `git clone`, `git pull`,
`git status`, `git add`, `git rm`, `git commit`, and `git push`. The first
clones a repository using an HTTPS URL or an SSH key; `pull` downloads and
integrates updates; `status` reports changed, staged, and untracked files and
whether the local branch is ahead of or behind its remote; `add` stages
selected changes; `rm` removes a file from the index and working tree; `commit`
records a snapshot with a message; and `push` sends commits to a remote. The
commands `git diff`, `git branch`, and `git reset` are useful for more advanced
work; use `git reset` only after learning how it changes history.

## Inspecting and Recovering History

Git's history commands let you understand a change before trying to undo it.
Use a compact log for the sequence of commits and a diff for exact lines:

```bash
git log --oneline --decorate --graph --all
git show COMMIT
git diff HEAD~1 HEAD
```

Different recovery commands have different safety implications. `git restore
path/to/file` discards unstaged edits, `git restore --staged path/to/file`
unstages a file without changing its contents, and `git revert COMMIT` creates
a new commit that reverses an earlier published commit. Avoid `git reset` on a
shared branch until you understand how it changes history.

## Branches and Remotes

A branch is a movable name for a line of commits. Branches let you develop and
review an idea without changing the shared default branch:

```bash
git switch -c improve-introduction
# edit files, then add and commit
git switch main
git pull --ff-only
git switch improve-introduction
```

A **remote** is a name for another repository, usually an online copy called
`origin`. These commands inspect and synchronize it:

```bash
git remote -v
git fetch origin
git pull --ff-only origin main
git push -u origin improve-introduction
```

`git fetch` downloads remote history without changing working files; `git pull`
fetches and then integrates the selected branch. Pull before starting work
when others may have pushed changes, and push completed commits so that a
second copy exists.

Git reports a conflict when two changes cannot be integrated automatically. Use
this sequence to resolve one:

```bash
git status                         # list conflicted files
# open each conflicted file and choose the intended content
# remove the <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> markers
git add path/to/resolved-file.qmd
git diff --staged                  # inspect the resolution
git commit                         # finish the merge, if Git requests it
```

Do not choose a side blindly. Ask the contributor who made the other change
when the intended result is unclear, and run the project's checks after the
resolution. If you need to abandon an unfinished merge, use `git merge
--abort` before making further edits.

## GitHub and Pull Requests

GitHub is a hosting and collaboration service, not a replacement for Git. A
repository on GitHub can store the canonical source, while each contributor
works in a local clone and exchanges commits through a remote.

A pull request proposes merging a branch into another branch. It gives
reviewers a place to inspect the diff, discuss design and evidence, and run
checks before the change is merged.

Small pull requests are easier to review and less likely to conceal an
accidental change. Include the motivation, files affected, and checks you ran;
do not include rendered `_book/` output when it is generated by the project.

GitHub's pull-request process is easiest to follow as a sequence of checks:

1. Fork the upstream repository and synchronize the fork if it is out of date.
2. Clone your fork and confirm that you can open the project in your editor.
3. Run `git status` to verify that the working tree is clean.
4. Create a descriptive branch, make the change, and run the relevant checks.
5. Run `git status` and inspect the diff before staging and committing.
6. Push the branch, open the pull request, and describe the change for
   reviewers.

GitHub provides a short [pull requests in 100 seconds
video](https://youtu.be/8lGpZkjnkt4), and its documentation explains the full
workflow [@github2025pullrequests].

For a class-notes contribution, the concrete command-line sequence looks like
this:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/GitHub_Username/ids-book.git
cd ids-book
git status
git switch -c branch-name
# edit a file, for example index.qmd, and save it
git status
git add index.qmd
git diff --staged
git commit -m "content: add a useful example"
git push -u origin branch-name
```

Replace `GitHub_Username` and `branch-name` with your own values. On GitHub,
open the fork, click **Compare & pull request**, describe the change, and click
**Create pull request**. If you are on the wrong branch, use `git switch
existing-branch`; use `git branch` to list branches and identify the current
one. Before beginning work, use **Sync fork** on GitHub when the fork is behind
the upstream repository.

## Practical Recommendations

The following checklist turns the chapter's concepts into everyday repository
habits:

- Use the command-line interface instead of the web interface for Git
  operations, such as uploading files to GitHub.
- Make frequent small commits instead of rare large commits.
- Make commit messages informative and meaningful.
- Name files and folders with lowercase letters and no spaces.
- Keep the repository clean by not tracking generated files.
- Create and maintain a `.gitignore` file for generated output, caches, local
  environments, and secrets.
- Keep source lines under 80 characters so that diffs remain readable.
- Run `git status` before and after important operations.
- Inspect a diff before staging and inspect the staged diff before committing.
- Pull before starting work when collaborators may have pushed changes, and
  push completed commits so that a second copy exists.

Git tracks text changes well but is not a data warehouse. Keep reproducible
scripts, small instructional data, and environment specifications under
version control; keep credentials, huge raw datasets, and generated results out
of the repository. Record where excluded data came from and how to obtain it
so another analyst can reproduce the work.

Use this file-level rule when deciding what belongs in a repository:

- **Track:** source code (`.py`, `.qmd`, and `.R`), documentation, small example
  data, configuration needed to reproduce the project, environment
  specifications, and `.gitignore`.
- **Do not track:** passwords, API keys, private keys, personal data, huge raw
  datasets, downloaded installers, temporary files, caches, virtual
  environments, rendered `_book/` output, or other files generated from the
  tracked source.

Put the exclusion rule in `.gitignore` before creating files that should not be
tracked. If sensitive information is accidentally committed, deleting the file
in a later commit does not remove it from the earlier history; change the
exposed credential and seek help to remove the history safely.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

Write one `.qmd` file containing your answers to all problems.

1. Establish a usable GitHub project from the command line.
   a. Create an account if necessary and configure SSH authentication, or explain
      why you selected HTTPS.
   b. Fork `statds/ids-book`, clone your fork, configure your name and email, and
      verify the remote, identity, and a clean `git status`.
   c. Record what failed and how you fixed it; do not omit an obstacle merely
      because you eventually solved it.

2. Make and review a reproducible contribution in your fork.
   a. Create and check out a descriptive branch, make a small documented change
      to a practice file, and make at least ten small commits with informative
      messages.
   b. Inspect both `git diff` and `git diff --staged` as you work, then push the
      branch to your fork.
   c. Open a pull request against the repository from which you forked, describe
      the change clearly, and respond to one review comment with a follow-up
      commit. Include enough setup information that another student can clone the
      fork and reproduce the result on their own computer.

3. Explain the conventions you used in a complete-paragraph `.qmd` report.
   a. Explain why a professional workflow uses the command line rather than web
      uploads, why binary and generated files stay out of Git, and why a homework
      PDF belongs in a GitHub release.
   b. Explain why this course requires lowercase names, 80-character source
      lines, and multiple small commits, using examples from your repository.
   c. Verify the final state with `git status` and include the commands and links
      needed for another student to inspect it.
